intro: The decorated melody stands above a bass and harmonic plan that will support thirty variations. This recording contains the complete opening Aria, with its two repeated halves, not the whole cycle.
question: Which part of an ornate melody’s accompaniment can become the foundation of thirty variations?

cues.title: Melody above a foundation
cues.text: The right hand ornaments a slow triple-metre melody while the bass moves more deliberately below it. In the complete cycle, the variations follow this bass and harmonic plan more consistently than they follow the Aria’s decorated tune.
cues.evidence: Mutopia 979, based on the Bach-Gesellschaft score, shows the 3/4 Aria and its independent bass. The Netherlands Bach Society explains the bass foundation of the cycle: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-988.

cues.title: A story told much later
cues.text: The story of music commissioned for Count Keyserlingk’s sleepless nights comes from Forkel’s Bach biography of 1802. The 1741 printed edition names neither the count nor Goldberg; the familiar title should not be mistaken for Bach’s documented dedication.
cues.evidence: Forkel’s later account and the absence of a dedication on the original title page are discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations and in the Netherlands Bach Society work account. The commission story is not presented as an established event.

cues.title: The first half repeats
cues.text: The first sixteen-bar half returns to its beginning after reaching D major. Listen again to the bass’s downward opening steps: repetition lets the ear learn the structure beneath the ornaments.
cues.evidence: The score has a repeat after bar 16; bass bars 1–4 descend G–F♯–E–D. The report marks boundaries at 1:10 and 1:14, followed by a pitch/attack pattern resembling the opening around 1:15–1:45. The 1:15 repeat point remains provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Music issued in print
cues.text: Balthasar Schmid published the variations in Nuremberg in 1741. The title specifies a harpsichord with two manuals; Shelley Katz performs this recording on piano, an instrumental choice distinct from that printed specification.
cues.evidence: Publication and two-manual specification are documented on the original edition’s title page, discussed at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations. Commons explicitly credits Shelley Katz as pianist; its 2012 date is not treated as an established session date.

cues.title: The second harmonic route
cues.text: The second half leaves the first half’s D-major cadence and moves through a more minor-coloured region before returning to G major. Follow the bass: the ornaments can obscure the change in direction if attention remains only on the top notes.
cues.evidence: Score bars 17–32 pass through E minor before recovering G major. The report has a low-level window at 2:25 and boundaries at 2:24 and 2:32, followed by E-minor material; the 2:26 map time is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An aria in the household
cues.text: Anna Magdalena Bach copied the Aria into the notebook begun in 1725. The entry itself is later: the date on the notebook does not prove that this music was composed in 1725.
cues.evidence: The source discussion at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldberg_Variations distinguishes the 1725 notebook from the later copied entry and cites Christoph Wolff’s dating around 1740. No exact copying day or composition year is asserted.

cues.title: The second half repeats
cues.text: The second half begins again after its return to G major. Compare this repetition’s overall weight with the first traversal, while keeping the same sequence of bass notes and cadences in mind.
cues.evidence: The score repeats bars 17–32. The report boundary at 3:38 begins a repeated E-minor-to-G-major contour and the later traversal has higher relative level. The timing is inferred from the score’s repeat and the report, not an asserted bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ornaments belong to the line
cues.text: Across the decorated melody, hear the small notes in relation to their destinations rather than as separate tunes. A trill or leaning note can delay arrival while the bass continues to define the phrase’s harmonic route.
cues.evidence: The score specifies trills, mordents and appoggiaturas throughout the Aria. No particular ornament is assigned to 4:15, and the report cannot distinguish Katz’s individual ornament realisations.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The piano’s final decay
cues.text: The closing sound recedes after the final G-major cadence. In the full cycle the Aria leads into Variation 1; this selected track ends here, leaving the complete variation sequence outside the recording.
cues.evidence: Relative level drops from −9.6 dB at 4:40 to −16.4 dB at 4:45 and −30.3 dB at 4:50, with no detected attacks in the last window. The source identifies this as track 01, Aria, not the complete cycle.

transitions.title: A dominant cadence leads back to G
transitions.how: The first half reaches D major, the dominant of G, then the written repeat returns directly to the opening G-major bass and decorated melody. There is no connecting bridge. Repeating the same sixteen bars lets the listener hear the bass descent and cadential route again; the performance can change its weight without changing the harmonic framework.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia/BGA Aria bars 1–16, with repeat at bar 16. The report boundaries near 1:10–1:14 and renewed opening pattern after 1:15 support an approximate repeat point; no single chord onset is aligned.

transitions.title: D major opens a different harmonic route
transitions.how: After the repeated first half closes in D major, the second half keeps the triple pulse and decorated melodic style but changes the bass’s route. Its harmonies move towards E minor before recovering G major later in the span. The join therefore changes tonal direction without changing instrument, metre or the distinction between ornate upper line and slower foundation.
transitions.evidence: Score bars 16–24 give the D-major close and the second half’s E-minor route. The report’s 2:24/2:32 boundaries surround the estimated 2:26 join; the following E-minor region supports, but does not independently establish, the written harmony.

transitions.title: The tonic close becomes a new departure
transitions.how: The second half reaches G major but the repeat sends the pianist back to its own beginning, not to the Aria’s opening bar. The same minor-coloured detour is therefore heard a second time before the final tonic cadence. Keeping the two repeat points distinct clarifies the design: each half retraces its own harmonic route.
transitions.evidence: The second repeat encloses score bars 17–32. A report boundary at 3:38 and the recurrence of the second half’s pitch and attack pattern support the 3:38 estimate; this is not an exact bar-aligned join.

facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
